headline: High risk of shared-workspace prompt injection and data leakage; both frameworks write/read files and use broad egress by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGen can read/write configured working directories and execute code; LangGraph can wire developer-defined tools and uses application-defined files. If they share a workspace, one agent can ingest the other’s file outputs as trusted content. No MCP/shared-channel is documented, so this is a workspace-mediated injection path rather than a proven direct bridge.
conditions: IF both agents are configured to use the same writable directory, injected instructions can traverse via files.
IF either agent parses the other’s generated files as prompts or tool instructions, hijack risk materializes.
mitigations: Use separate per-agent directories.
Prefix all inter-agent files with machine-readable schemas.
Add a manual review step before one agent consumes the other’s output.
Disable automatic prompt ingestion from shared files.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags and content filtering at the orchestrator boundary.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents can read files and send requests to model providers; AutoGen explicitly handles model provider API keys, and LangGraph can call developer-defined tools. In a shared workspace, sensitive application data touched by one agent can be exposed to the other and then uploaded to inference backends. This is a default-configuration risk if the operator co-locates them.
conditions: IF both agents share a workspace containing sensitive files, either can read them.
IF either agent forwards file contents to a model provider, those contents can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Separate sensitive and non-sensitive workspaces.
Restrict file permissions so each agent sees only its own inputs.
Turn off automatic file attachment to prompts.
Use local-only models for sensitive runs.
requires-engineering: enforce egress allowlists and DLP scanning on tool outputs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write and shell execution, and LangGraph’s shared_state_with_other_instances uses a checkpointer store while AutoGen supports multiple instances with developer-defined shared state. If they target the same mutable directory or state store, concurrent writes can corrupt files or state without locking. The overlap is broad and dangerous by default when co-deployed.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, file clobbering can occur.
IF both agents share a checkpointer or state backend without locks, state races can occur.
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories.
Use per-agent lock files around shared resources.
Serialize writes through one coordinator.
Avoid shared git or database state unless locked.
requires-engineering: add transactional locking to the shared state backend.

D_cascading_error.rationale: LangGraph is a graph of nodes where each node may itself be an agent, and AutoGen is a multi-agent group-chat framework that can emit tool calls and code execution. If LangGraph consumes AutoGen outputs without verification, errors or hallucinated facts can cascade into downstream actions. The pair’s default orchestration patterns make unverified handoff plausible and potentially harmful.
conditions: IF LangGraph routes AutoGen output directly into action nodes, mistakes can trigger downstream side effects.
IF AutoGen-generated facts are treated as authoritative without validation, error propagation occurs.
mitigations: Insert a verification node between agents.
Require structured outputs with schema validation.
Gate side-effecting tools behind human approval.
Log and diff intermediate claims before execution.
requires-engineering: add automated fact-checking against source data.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and docs-only, with no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch documented. The main compliance concern is operator configuration: AutoGen handles model provider API keys and LangGraph can use developer-defined tools, but the profiles do not prove a specific regulatory breach pathway. I therefore keep this low and avoid assuming undocumented obligations.
conditions: IF the operator routes regulated data through a noncompliant model provider or tool, compliance risk increases.
IF retention or residency settings differ across the two deployments, policy mismatch can occur.
mitigations: Document the data classes each agent may process.
Align retention settings across both deployments.
Use approved providers for regulated data.
Review vendor DPAs before enabling sensitive workloads.
requires-engineering: implement policy enforcement for residency and retention.
